decision.reason: While Smaby et al. (2007; 10.1002/bin.242, shipped row 2318) developed and validated the multiple-schedule reinforcer assessment (MSA) protocol itself, Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013; 10.1002/jaba.67) applied Smaby et al.'s MSA procedure to test a substantive empirical finding: the relative reinforcing efficacy of tokens plus praise versus either alone under differential reinforcement contingencies to reduce prompt dependency. Fiske et al. (2019) borrow Cividini-Motta and Ahearn's arbitrary two-star pointing task and fixed ascending component order to evaluate a different set of token-economy schedule contrasts (extinction, token delivery without backup exchange, yoked FR primary reinforcement, token delivery with backup exchange, and FR-1 primary edible/leisure reinforcement) with no praise condition and no prompt-dependency contingency. In the Results and Discussion, Fiske et al. compare their substantive schedule findings and assessment duration (26–36 min vs. 1 hr 28 min–2 hr 29 min) against prior token-component evaluations (Fiske et al., 2015; Leon et al., 2016) and note only that they used a task similar to Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013) and found the MSA protocol suitable. Adopting an earlier applicator's task/component order without retesting its empirical finding does not make Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013) a separate replication target beyond the MSA origin paper (Smaby et al., 2007).
